title: One-Way Analysis of Variance
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter addresses how to determine whether a continuous response differs across three or more treatment groups without inflating the false positive rate. It introduces the one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) framework as a linear regression model with dummy variables, details the omnibus $F$-test based on sum of squares decompositions, and examines post-hoc multiple comparison corrections using the Bonferroni and Tukey methods. Familiarity with simple linear regression, the two-sample $t$-test, and basic hypothesis testing is assumed. --- ## The Multi-Group Comparison Problem Consider an experiment designed to assess the biological impact of arachidonic acid on plasma concentrations of prostacyclin, a vasodilatory lipid that inhibits platelet activation and prevents blood clotting. Researchers administered arachidonic acid to rats across three distinct concentration levels: - Low dose ($L$, 10 units) - Medium dose ($M$, 25 units) - High dose ($H$, 50 units) The experimental design is a completely randomized design (CRD): 36 rats were assigned at random, with $n_1 = n_2 = n_3 = 12$ rats per treatment group. The outcome variable $Y$ is the prostacyclin concentration in blood plasma measured in $\text{ng/ml}$. Let $g$ denote the number of groups (here $g=3$). We assume within each group $j \in \{1, \dots, g\}$, the observations are normally distributed around a group-specific mean $\mu_j$, sharing a common variance $\sigma^2$: $$ Y_i \mid \text{group } j \sim N(\mu_j, \sigma^2) $$ The scientific question is whether the administered dose affects mean prostacyclin levels. Statistically, this translates to testing whether all group means are identical against the alternative that at least one group differs: $$ H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_g $$ $$ H_1: \exists \, j, k \in \{1, \dots, g\} \text{ such that } \mu_j \neq \mu_k $$ A naive approach would evaluate this question by splitting $H_0$ into pairwise hypotheses: $$ H_{0jk}: \mu_j = \mu_k \quad \text{versus} \quad H_{1jk}: \mu_j \neq \mu_k $$ and testing each pair using a two-sample $t$-test. However, testing multiple hypotheses simultaneously creates a severe multiplicity problem: the probability of committing at least one Type I error across the set of tests inflates well above the nominal significance level $\alpha$. Furthermore, performing pairwise tests independently fails to exploit the full dataset to estimate the shared variance $\sigma^2$, causing a loss of statistical power. **Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)** solves this problem by assessing the omnibus hypothesis $H_0$ through a single statistical test. --- ## One-Way ANOVA as a Linear Model Just as a two-sample comparison can be formulated as a linear regression with an indicator variable, a comparison across $g$ groups can be expressed via multiple linear regression using $g - 1$ dummy variables. Choosing the low-dose group ($L$) as the **reference group**, we define two indicator variables for the remaining groups: $$ x_{i1} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if observation } i \text{ belongs to the medium dose group } (M) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ $$ x_{i2} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if observation } i \text{ belongs to the high dose group } (H) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ The linear regression model is: $$ Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \epsilon_i, \quad \epsilon_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2) $$ Writing the expectation $\text{E}[Y_i]$ for each group reveals the interpretation of the coefficients: - **Group $L$ ($x_{i1} = 0, x_{i2} = 0$):** $$\text{E}[Y_i \mid L] = \beta_0 = \mu_1$$ - **Group $M$ ($x_{i1} = 1, x_{i2} = 0$):** $$\text{E}[Y_i \mid M] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 = \mu_2 \implies \beta_1 = \mu_2 - \mu_1$$ - **Group $H$ ($x_{i1} = 0, x_{i2} = 1$):** $$\text{E}[Y_i \mid H] = \beta_0 + \beta_2 = \mu_3 \implies \beta_2 = \mu_3 - \mu_1$$ Here, $\beta_0$ represents the mean prostacyclin concentration in the baseline condition (dose 10), while $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ represent the treatment effects of doses 25 and 50 relative to baseline. Under this parameterization, the global null hypothesis $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_3$ is equivalent to: $$ H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = 0 $$ versus the alternative hypothesis: $$ H_1: \beta_1 \neq 0 \quad \text{or} \quad \beta_2 \neq 0 $$ --- ## Sums of Squares and the ANOVA Decomposition Testing $H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = 0$ compares the full model predictions against a reduced model containing only the intercept $\beta_0$ (estimated by the grand mean $\bar{Y}$). The total variability of the observations about the grand mean is partitioned into two orthogonal components: $$ \text{SSTot} = \text{SST} + \text{SSE} $$ ### 1. Total Sum of Squares ($\text{SSTot}$) The total variation across all $n$ observations ($n = \sum_{j=1}^g n_j$): $$ \text{SSTot} = \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2 $$ $\text{SSTot}$ has $n - 1$ degrees of freedom because one degree of freedom is lost estimating the grand sample mean $\bar{Y}$. ### 2. Treatment Sum of Squares ($\text{SST}$) Also known as the *between-group sum of squares* ($\text{SS}_{\text{Between}}$) or regression sum of squares ($\text{SSR}$). It measures deviations of group-specific predictions $\hat{Y}_i = \bar{Y}_j$ from the grand mean $\bar{Y}$: $$ \text{SST} = \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2 = \sum_{j=1}^g n_j (\bar{Y}_j - \bar{Y})^2 $$ For the prostacyclin experiment with equal group sizes $n_1 = n_2 = n_3 = 12$: $$ \text{SST} = 12(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y})^2 + 12(\bar{Y}_2 - \bar{Y})^2 + 12(\bar{Y}_3 - \bar{Y})^2 $$ $\text{SST}$ carries $g - 1$ degrees of freedom (here $3 - 1 = 2$). If $H_0$ is true, the sample means $\bar{Y}_j$ will differ from $\bar{Y}$ only due to random sampling fluctuations, yielding $\text{SST} \approx 0$. If treatment effects exist, $\text{SST}$ grows large. ### 3. Error Sum of Squares ($\text{SSE}$) Also referred to as the *residual sum of squares* or *within-group sum of squares* ($\text{SS}_{\text{Within}}$). It quantifies variation within each treatment group: $$ \text{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2 = \sum_{j=1}^g \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_j)^2 = \sum_{j=1}^g (n_j - 1) S_j^2 $$ where $S_j^2$ is the sample variance in group $j$. $\text{SSE}$ carries $\sum_{j=1}^g (n_j - 1) = n - g$ degrees of freedom (here $36 - 3 = 33$). --- ## The $F$-Test and the ANOVA Table Dividing each sum of squares by its associated degrees of freedom produces the **mean squares**: - **Mean Square for Treatments:** $$\text{MST} = \frac{\text{SST}}{g - 1}$$ - **Mean Square for Error:** $$\text{MSE} = \frac{\text{SSE}}{n - g} = \sum_{j=1}^g \frac{(n_j - 1)S_j^2}{n - g}$$ $\text{MSE}$ is an unbiased estimator of the residual variance $\sigma^2$ regardless of whether $H_0$ holds, pooling variance information across all $g$ groups. $\text{MST}$ estimates $\sigma^2$ if $H_0$ is true, but additionally captures group differences if $H_0$ is false. The test statistic is the ratio: $$ F = \frac{\text{MST}}{\text{MSE}} = \frac{\text{variability between groups}}{\text{variability within groups}} $$ Under the null hypothesis and standard assumptions (normality, independence, and homoscedasticity across groups): $$ F \sim F_{g-1, \, n-g} $$ Large values of $F$ indicate that group means deviate from each other more than expected by within-group random error alone. At significance level $\alpha$, $H_0$ is rejected if $F \ge F_{1-\alpha, \, g-1, \, n-g}$. The components of this test are compiled into an **ANOVA Table**: | Source of Variation | Degrees of Freedom ($\text{Df}$) | Sum of Squares ($\text{Sum Sq}$) | Mean Square ($\text{Mean Sq}$) | $F$-value | $p$-value | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Treatment** | $g - 1$ | $\text{SST}$ | $\text{MST} = \frac{\text{SST}}{g-1}$ | $\frac{\text{MST}}{\text{MSE}}$ | $\text{P}(F_{g-1, n-g} \ge F)$ | | **Residuals (Error)** | $n - g$ | $\text{SSE}$ | $\text{MSE} = \frac{\text{SSE}}{n-g}$ | | | ### Prostacyclin Empirical Results Fitting the linear model to the prostacyclin dataset in R yields: ```r model1 <- lm(prostac ~ dose, data = prostacyclin) summary(model1) ``` ``` Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 40.108 6.150 6.521 2.10e-07 *** dose25 8.258 8.698 0.949 0.349 dose50 43.258 8.698 4.974 1.99e-05 *** --- Residual standard error: 21.3 on 33 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.458, Adjusted R-squared: 0.4252 F-statistic: 13.94 on 2 and 33 DF, p-value: 4.081e-05 ``` The corresponding ANOVA table is: ```r anova(model1) ``` ``` Analysis of Variance Table Response: prostac Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) dose 2 12658.0 6329.0 13.944 4.081e-05 *** Residuals 33 14979.0 453.9 ``` From this output: - $\text{MST} = 12658.0 / 2 = 6329.0$ - $\text{MSE} = 14979.0 / 33 = 453.9$ - $F = 6329.0 / 453.9 = 13.944$ With a $p$-value of $4.081 \times 10^{-5} \ll 0.001$, the omnibus test provides strong evidence against $H_0$, establishing that arachidonic acid dose significantly affects plasma prostacyclin levels. --- ## Post-Hoc Analysis: Multiplicity and Family-Wise Error Rate Rejecting the omnibus null hypothesis confirms that not all group means are equal, but it does not specify *which* specific pairs of treatments differ. Answering this requires post-hoc comparisons between pairs of means: $$ H_{0jk}: \mu_j = \mu_k \quad \text{versus} \quad H_{1jk}: \mu_j \neq \mu_k $$ Using the pooled variance estimate $\text{MSE}$ from the full ANOVA model, pairwise test statistics take the form: $$ T_{jk} = \frac{\bar{Y}_j - \bar{Y}_k}{\sqrt{\text{MSE} \left( \frac{1}{n_j} + \frac{1}{n_k} \right)}} \sim t_{n-g} $$ ### The Inflation of Multiplicity Testing $g$ groups involves $m = \binom{g}{2} = \frac{g(g-1)}{2}$ pairwise comparisons. If each comparison is conducted at nominal significance level $\alpha$, and assuming independence between tests: $$ \text{FWER} = \text{P}(\text{at least one Type I error}) = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^m $$ When $\alpha = 0.05$: - For $g = 3$ ($m = 3$ tests): $\text{FWER} = 1 - (0.95)^3 \approx 0.143$ - For $g = 5$ ($m = 10$ tests): $\text{FWER} = 1 - (0.95)^{10} \approx 0.401$ Simulation under $H_0$ with correlated $t$-statistics produces empirical Type I error rates of $12.1\%$ for $g=3$ and $28.0\%$ for $g=5$, confirming substantial inflation above $5\%$. Controlling this false positive inflation requires guarding the **Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER)** at an experiment-wise level $\alpha_E$ (typically 0.05). ### 1. The Bonferroni Correction By Boole's inequality, the probability of a union of events is bounded by the sum of their individual probabilities: $$ \text{P}\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^m E_k\right) \le \sum_{k=1}^m \text{P}(E_k) \le m\alpha $$ To ensure $\text{FWER} \le \alpha_E$, the Bonferroni method tests each individual comparison at: $$ \alpha = \frac{\alpha_E}{m} $$ Equivalently, individual $p$-values are multiplied by the number of comparisons $m$: $$ \tilde{p}_{jk} = \min(m \cdot p_{jk}, \, 1) $$ Bonferroni-adjusted simultaneous $(1 - \alpha_E)100\%$ confidence intervals are given by: $$ (\bar{Y}_j - \bar{Y}_k) \pm t_{1 - \frac{\alpha_E}{2m}, \, n-g} \sqrt{\text{MSE} \left( \frac{1}{n_j} + \frac{1}{n_k} \right)} $$ Applying this to the prostacyclin data ($m = 3$ comparisons, critical multiplier $t_{1 - 0.05/6, \, 33} = 2.5222$): ```r library(multcomp) model1.mcp <- glht(model1, linfct = mcp(dose = "Tukey")) summary(model1.mcp, test = adjusted("bonferroni")) ``` ``` Linear Hypotheses: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) 25 - 10 == 0 8.258 8.698 0.949 1.000000 50 - 10 == 0 43.258 8.698 4.974 5.98e-05 *** 50 - 25 == 0 35.000 8.698 4.024 0.000943 *** (Adjusted p values reported -- bonferroni method) ``` The Bonferroni method provides rigorous protection against Type I errors, but its conservative nature leads to a loss of statistical power, generating an empirical FWER of $4.6\%$ for $g=3$ and $4.1\%$ for $g=5$ under nominal $\alpha_E = 0.05$. ### 2. Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) Tukey's method avoids the conservative nature of the Bonferroni bound by relying on the distribution of the **studentized range statistic**: $$ Q = \frac{\max_j(\bar{Y}_j) - \min_j(\bar{Y}_j)}{\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{n_0}}} $$ where $n_0$ is the common sample size per group. Tukey contrasts evaluate simultaneous pairwise differences using critical values derived from the exact joint distribution of all pairwise differences under $H_0$. Applying Tukey contrasts to the prostacyclin data: ```r summary(model1.mcp) ``` ``` Linear Hypotheses: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) 25 - 10 == 0 8.258 8.698 0.949 0.613390 50 - 10 == 0 43.258 8.698 4.974 < 1e-04 *** 50 - 25 == 0 35.000 8.698 4.024 0.000835 *** (Adjusted p values reported -- single-step method) ``` Simultaneous $95\%$ family-wise confidence intervals (critical quantile $2.4539$): ```r confint(model1.mcp) ``` ``` Linear Hypotheses: Estimate lwr upr 25 - 10 == 0 8.2583 -13.0849 29.6016 50 - 10 == 0 43.2583 21.9151 64.6016 50 - 25 == 0 35.0000 13.6567 56.3433 ``` Tukey's method yields narrower confidence intervals and smaller adjusted $p$-values than Bonferroni while holding empirical FWER precisely at nominal levels ($5.03\%$ for $g=3$; $5.2\%$ for $g=5$ in simulation). --- ## Synthesis of the Prostacyclin Analysis A complete analysis follows a structured two-stage workflow: first checking the omnibus ANOVA $F$-test, followed by multiplicity-adjusted post-hoc comparisons. 1. **Omnibus Analysis:** The one-way ANOVA indicates a highly significant overall treatment effect of arachidonic acid dose on prostacyclin levels ($F_{2, 33} = 13.94$, $p < 0.001$). 2. **Post-Hoc Pairwise Comparisons (Tukey Adjusted):** - High dose (50 units) versus Low dose (10 units): mean increase of $43.3 \text{ ng/ml}$ ($95\% \text{ CI: } [21.9, 64.6]$, adjusted $p < 0.001$). - High dose (50 units) versus Medium dose (25 units): mean increase of $35.0 \text{ ng/ml}$ ($95\% \text{ CI: } [13.7, 56.3]$, adjusted $p < 0.001$). - Medium dose (25 units) versus Low dose (10 units): estimated difference of $8.3 \text{ ng/ml}$ ($95\% \text{ CI: } [-13.1, 29.6]$, adjusted $p = 0.613$). The biological conclusion is that prostacyclin levels rise substantially at the highest arachidonic acid dose (50 units), whereas the difference between the low (10 units) and medium (25 units) doses is not statistically distinguishable from zero. --- ## Sources - **Section 7.1 Inleiding**: Experimental design of the prostacyclin study, CRD setup, normality and homoscedasticity assumptions, and initial formulation of hypotheses $H_0$ and $H_1$. - **Section 7.2 Variantie-analyse**: Linear dummy regression reparameterization, sum of squares decomposition ($\text{SSTot} = \text{SST} + \text{SSE}$), derivation of degrees of freedom, mean squares, the omnibus $F$-test, and the ANOVA table. - **Section 7.3 Post hoc analyse: Meervoudig Vergelijken van Gemiddelden**: Multiplicity demonstrations, pairwise pooled $t$-tests, definition of Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER), and the derivation and application of Bonferroni and Tukey HSD adjustments. - **Section 7.4 Conclusies: Prostacycline Voorbeeld**: Synthesis of the two-stage analytical procedure and biological reporting of results.
